tip: 'Kunci inggris', literally 'English key', is the everyday Indonesian word for a wrench – 'kunci' alone just means key or lock.
'Se-' + adjective = 'as X as': 'setinggi lutut' = knee-high, 'sebesar rumah' = as big as a house.
'Semakin' X, 'semakin' Y = 'the more X, the more Y': 'semakin lama, semakin sulit'.
'Ke-...-an' on adjectives names the state: 'kering' dry, 'kekeringan' drought; 'aman' safe, 'keamanan' safety.
'Ke-...-an' also makes nouns from verbs: 'memutuskan' decide, 'keputusan' decision; 'sempat' manage to, 'kesempatan' chance.
'Justru' flips an expectation: 'actually, on the contrary'. 'Gagal justru membuat saya berani' = failing actually made me brave.
'Saling' + verb = 'each other': 'saling menghormati' = respect each other. No object needed.
'Lama' means 'a long time'; doubled, 'lama-lama' means 'eventually, given enough time': 'lama-lama terasa hasilnya' – in time you feel the results.
'Bukan' negates nouns, 'tidak' negates verbs and adjectives: 'bukan satu orang saja' = not just one person.
'Ketinggalan' = left behind, or 'to miss' transport: 'ketinggalan kereta' = to miss the train.
'Betapa' = 'how...!' in exclamations: 'betapa pentingnya' = how important (it is).
'Buah tangan' – literally 'fruit of the hand' – is the small gift you bring when visiting someone's home. Arriving empty-handed can read as impolite.
'Jangan sampai' = 'don't let it get to the point that': 'jangan sampai terlambat' = don't end up late.
'Pun' after a noun = 'even': 'cangkir yang pecah pun' = even a broken cup.
Adding '-lah' softens a command into an invitation: 'bawalah jas hujan' = do bring a raincoat.
'Agar' = 'supaya' = 'so that': 'memperingatkan agar tidak berenang' = warn (them) not to swim.
'Bergotong royong' comes from 'gotong royong' – neighbors pitching in together unpaid – a named core value of Indonesian village life.
'Padahal' = 'and yet, even though': 'rusak lagi, padahal baru diperbaiki' = broken again, yet just fixed.
Responsibility is carried in Indonesian: 'tanggung jawab yang harus kamu pikul' = responsibility you must shoulder – 'pikul' = carry on the shoulder.
'Merantau' = leaving home to make a living elsewhere; 'perantauan' is that faraway place. A big theme in Indonesian life.
'Diturunkan' = 'passed down' (lit. lowered): 'diturunkan dari generasi ke generasi' = passed down from generation to generation.
'Ada gula ada semut' – 'where there's sugar there are ants': people gather wherever there's money or good fortune. A stock comment on crowds.
'Sedikit demi sedikit, lama-lama menjadi bukit' – little by little it becomes a hill. The standard Indonesian proverb for slow, steady saving.
'Bagai pinang dibelah dua' – 'like a betel nut split in two': two people identical in looks. Said of twins or striking lookalikes.
'Sekali mendayung, dua tiga pulau terlampaui' – one paddle stroke passes two or three islands: one effort, several goals. The Indonesian 'two birds, one stone'.
'Air tenang menghanyutkan' – calm water sweeps you away: quiet people can be the most formidable. The Indonesian take on 'still waters run deep'.
A classic 'pantun' (traditional rhyme) most Indonesians know: 'bersakit-sakit dahulu, bersenang-senang kemudian' – suffer first, enjoy later. Hard work pays off in the end.
'Tak kenal maka tak sayang' – 'unknown means unloved'. Indonesians quote it when introducing something new: get to know it and you'll come to like it.
'Di mana bumi dipijak, di situ langit dijunjung' – where you stand, hold up that sky: follow local customs wherever you are. The Indonesian 'when in Rome'.
'Nasi sudah menjadi bubur' – the rice has already become porridge: it can't be undone, so deal with what's next. The Indonesian 'no crying over spilled milk'.
